title: I made a free old-school gothic beat 'em up where you play Dracula (hand-painted, made with Godot)
author: Individual_Battle686
selftext:
Hi everyone! This is my first public build of **Dracula, le Chasseur de la nuit** (*Dracula, Hunter of the Night*).

* Level 1: brawl through a harbour town, bite the townsfolk, turn into a bat, unleash a swarm of bats, and reap souls to become the Super Vampire, before facing the Captain and the beast he becomes.
* Level 2: a night ride on horseback: jump hedges and streams, dodge logs and hay bales, fight off wolf packs and the Baron's riders.

It's free (Windows and Android, gamepad recommended). It's still early and unfinished, so I'd love your honest feedback: what works, what doesn't, how far you got.

[https://flibustier54.itch.io/dracula-le-chasseur-de-la-nuit](https://flibustier54.itch.io/dracula-le-chasseur-de-la-nuit)

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body: u/Individual_Battle686 please expand this post with how you used AI during development. It's not enough to say you used AI. Tell us what you did with it. The point of Rule 4 is for promotional posts to give something back by sharing the process and actual development. We're cracking down on posts that only advertise. If you don't update, this may be removed.

replies.author: Individual_Battle686
replies.body:
Thanks, fair point! Here’s how AI was actually used, step by step.

**Who did what**  
I’m a solo hobbyist. I designed the game, the characters, the levels and the rules, and I play-tested everything. I don’t draw or code professionally, so I used AI tools as my “team” and spent most of my time directing and correcting them.

**Art (ChatGPT image generation)**

* Every character, animation and backdrop was generated with ChatGPT, but never in one shot. I wrote a long rulebook (now \~130 sections) that I attach to every request: body proportions measured in “heads” (7.5 heads tall, hips at mid-height), a skeleton drawn first, and limbs color-coded (right arm blue, left arm red, right leg green, left leg orange) so the AI can’t swap arms or legs between frames.
* AI loves to mirror hands, twist knees backwards or add fingers, so each delivery is checked frame by frame and sent back when it’s wrong.
* Everything is delivered in separate layers: the horse, the rider, the far leg, each held object. That way Godot can animate a sword, a chain or a thrown object by itself instead of redrawing it in every frame.
* Backgrounds that touch each other are painted as one piece and then cut in two, so there’s no visible seam when the level scrolls.
* For realism (a horse’s gallop, a wolf’s run with real airborne phases), I first look at slow-motion reference videos and give the measured phases to the AI.

**Code (Claude Code)**  
The game runs in Godot 4. Claude Code wrote the GDScript from my instructions, then we iterated a lot. Example: wolves “sliding” on the ground led to a redrawn 12-frame gallop with airborne phases, plus optical-flow interpolation to double the frame count.

**Music (Suno)**  
Medieval and gothic tracks generated with Suno, picked and edited by me.

**Cutscenes**  
Manga-style panels generated as images, then assembled and timed into videos, with my own text captions.

**What I learned**  
AI doesn’t imagine anything for you, and it doesn’t keep a character consistent on its own. The real work is in the rules, the checking, and saying “no, redo it” a hundred times. Without a clear vision, you get a pile of pretty but unusable pictures.

Happy to answer any question about the process!
